2027-06-16.title: Fifth Wednesday of the Apostles

2027-06-16.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. Today the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church begins the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu).
2027-06-16.verse: But law came in, with the result that the trespass multiplied; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,
theo: In the fifth chapter of Romans Paul sets the whole of human history between two men. “Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death came through sin, and so death spread to all because all have sinned…” The one man is Adam. Through his disobedience sin entered our race like a poison entering the bloodstream, and with sin came death, the separation that God never willed. The Church reads in this passage the revealed basis of her teaching on original sin: we are born into a wounded humanity, deprived of the holiness in which Adam was created, and every personal sin adds to the wound. But Paul's purpose is not to frighten us with Adam; it is to dazzle us with Christ. Adam, he says, “is a type of the one who was to come.” He is like a rough sketch of the true Man. And the comparison is not equal. Again and again Paul writes “much more”: if many died through one man's trespass, “much more surely have the grace of God” and his gift “abounded for the many.” Then the great parallel: “Therefore just as one man’s trespass led to condemnation for all, so one man’s act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all. For just as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.” Adam reached for the fruit of the tree to become like God; Christ, who is God, stretched out his arms on the tree of the Cross in obedience. Our own Mar Aprem, whom we remembered last week, loved to sing of the two trees, the tree of Eden and the tree of Golgotha, and of the Second Adam who opened again the gate of Paradise.

Then Paul writes one of the most consoling sentences in the Bible: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.” God's grace is not a small repair that barely covers the damage. It overflows. No sin of ours, no history of a family, no darkness of a nation is deeper than the grace of Christ. Paul will immediately warn that this is no excuse to go on sinning (Romans 6:1–2); grace that abounds is grace that changes us. But it means that no one in the parish, in the prison or in the hospital bed is beyond hope.

The Gospel tells the same story as a parable. Jesus speaks in the Temple, in the last days before his Passion, to the chief priests, the scribes and the elders who had questioned his authority (Mark 11:27). “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the wine press, and built a watchtower; then he leased it to tenants and went to another country.” His hearers knew Isaiah's song of the vineyard, in which the vineyard is God's people (Isaiah 5:1–7). The owner sends servant after servant to collect his share of the fruit; they are beaten, insulted, killed. The patience of the owner is almost foolish. “He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’” The word “beloved” is the word the Father spoke over Jesus at the Jordan and on the mountain (Mark 1:11; 9:7). But the tenants reason: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” Jesus is telling his own story, and he knows how it will end. Yet he ends with the psalm: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is amazing in our eyes.” The greatest sin ever committed, the rejection and killing of the Son, became the cornerstone of our salvation. Here is Paul's “where sin increased, grace abounded” in the shape of a story. The parable was spoken to particular leaders at a particular hour, and Mark says that the crowd was on Jesus' side; the Church has always refused to turn it into a verdict on the Jewish people, then or now (Nostra Aetate 4). It is addressed to us, the tenants of the vineyard today. Our parish, our family, our own life are leased to us by the Owner, who still sends his messengers looking for fruit. As our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters begin the Apostles' Fast today, the question is for all of us: what fruit will the Owner find?

live: If a sin has weighed on you for a long time, bring it this week to the sacrament of Reconciliation and believe that grace is greater.
Choose one fruit to give God this week: an hour of prayer, a reconciliation, an alms, or a visit to someone alone.
fathers: As through the disobedience of one man, formed from untilled earth, the many were made sinners and lost life, so through the obedience of one Man, born of the Virgin, the many are justified and receive salvation. The Word recapitulated Adam in himself, so that what we had lost in Adam we might recover in Christ Jesus.

Christ did not only pay what we owed; he gave far more. It is as if someone found a man in prison for a small debt, paid it, and then not only set him at liberty but gave him a great fortune, made him his own son and seated him on a royal throne. Such is the grace that abounds where sin abounded.
magis: All men are implicated in Adam's sin, as St Paul affirms (Romans 5:12, 19); original sin is a deprivation of original holiness and justice, transmitted with human nature, and it is called sin only in an analogical sense: it is contracted, not committed.

Why did God not prevent the first man from sinning? St Leo the Great answers: Christ's inexpressible grace gave us blessings better than those the demon's envy had taken away. Nothing prevents human nature being raised to something greater after sin, as St Paul says: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.

The historical complexity of Jesus' trial must be respected; neither all Jews indiscriminately at that time, nor Jews today, can be charged with the crimes committed during his Passion. The Church teaches that sinners were the authors of Christ's sufferings, and that Christians bear the gravest responsibility.
saints: No saint's memorial is kept in the Syro-Malabar or the Latin calendar today. In the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins today and ends on the feast of Sts Peter and Paul (29 June).

13–18 June: the fifth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 13: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles (in the Latin calendar the memorial of St Antony of Padua gives way to the Sunday). Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius are listed in the calendar. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Ahead: Thu 24 June, the Birth of John the Baptist; Tue 29 June, Sts Peter and Paul, a day of obligation.
2027-06-16.prayer: Lord God, through one man's disobedience sin and death entered the world, and through the obedience of your Son, the Second Adam, grace and life have abounded for all. You planted your vineyard with love and sent your servants and at last your beloved Son, whom we rejected; yet you made the rejected stone the cornerstone of our salvation. Where sin has increased in our lives, let your grace abound all the more. Make us faithful tenants of your vineyard, giving you the fruit you seek. Bless our Syro-Malankara brothers and sisters in their fast. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The beloved Son, thrown out of the vineyard and killed, is present on the altar as the cornerstone of the Church. The Blood that the tenants shed has become the cup of salvation.
At every Holy Qurbana the obedience of the Second Adam is offered for the many, and grace abounds where sin increased.

Paul: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.

2027-06-16.action: Give God one concrete fruit this week, and go to confession if a long-held sin weighs on you.
2027-06-16.question: What fruit will the Owner find when he comes to the vineyard of my life?

family.explain: Jesus told a story. A man planted a vineyard and gave it to some workers to look after. When it was time for the grapes, he sent helpers to collect his share, but the workers beat them and sent them away. Last of all he sent his own dear son, and they killed him. Jesus was talking about himself: God the Father sent his Son, Jesus, and he was killed on the Cross. But God turned that terrible thing into our salvation: the stone that was thrown away became the most important stone of the building. God can bring good even out of the worst things.
family.intention: We pray for anyone who has done something very wrong, that they may know God's forgiveness.
family.ask: Ask: “What good fruit can our family give to God this week?”

illus: In 1995 a young Franciscan Clarist sister from Kerala, Rani Maria Vattalil, who worked among the poor in Madhya Pradesh, was stabbed to death on a bus by a man named Samundar Singh. Years later her own sister, also a religious sister, went to visit him in prison. On the festival of Raksha Bandhan she tied a rakhi on his wrist and called him her brother. Her mother and family forgave him. The man who had killed a servant of God wept, asked forgiveness and changed his life. When Sister Rani Maria was beatified in Indore in 2017, he was there among those who honoured her. Where sin had increased, grace abounded all the more.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, beloved Son of the Father, you were rejected and you became the cornerstone. We come to you with our sins and our fruits. Let your grace abound in us, and send your Holy Spirit upon us as we pray. Amen.
share: Sin came into the world through one man (Romans 5:12). Where do I see the wound of sin in myself and in the world?
Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20). Where have I seen grace overflow after sin?
He sent a slave to the tenants to collect… his share of the produce (Mark 12:2). What fruit is God asking of me?
The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Mark 12:10). What has God built from what was rejected in my life?
pm.resp: Lord, let your grace abound in us.
interc: For the Church, the vineyard of the Lord, that she may bear abundant fruit in this Season of the Apostles.
For the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church as she begins the Apostles' Fast, and for all the Churches that keep this fast.
For those who have committed grave sins and for those in prison, that they may know that grace is greater.
For victims of violence and their families, that they may find healing and the strength to forgive.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, that they may grow in faithfulness to his covenant.
pm.close: Father, you sent your beloved Son to your vineyard and he was rejected, yet you made him the cornerstone. Let your grace abound where our sin has increased, and make us bear the fruit you seek. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul tells the whole story of humanity in two men. Through Adam, sin and death came into the world. Through Jesus Christ, grace and life came. We all share Adam's wound; we can all share Christ's healing.

And the two are not equal. Paul says again and again, “much more.” Grace is much stronger than sin. “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). There is no sin so great that the grace of Christ cannot overcome it.

In the Gospel Jesus tells a story about a vineyard. The owner sends servant after servant to collect the fruit, and the tenants beat them and kill them. At last he sends his beloved son, and they kill him too. Jesus is speaking about himself, the beloved Son of the Father, who will soon be put to death.

But God does not let the story end there. “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Mark 12:10). The worst thing human beings ever did, killing the Son of God, became the foundation of our salvation. That is what grace does: it turns even death into life.

Today we are the tenants of God's vineyard: our family, our parish, our own life. The Owner is looking for fruit. Let us give him the fruit of prayer, forgiveness and charity, and if we have sinned, let us run to his grace, which is always greater. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus told a story about a man who sent his own dear son to his vineyard, and bad workers killed him. Jesus was talking about himself. But God made something wonderful out of it: Jesus rose again and saved us! God can bring good even out of bad things. And God's love is always bigger than our sins.
